newsitem.title: USA: Mouse model may aid study of pregnancy complication.
newsitem.headline: Mouse model may aid study of pregnancy complication.

text.p: About one in 10 pregnancies bring complications from high blood pressure and Japanese scientists on Thursday said they had developed a mouse model that may lead to new understanding and perhaps treatments.

Pregnancy-induced hypertension (PIH) usually emerges in the final trimester. Also known as pre-eclampsia, it can send the woman's blood pressure soaring and in severe cases can endanger both her life and that of the foetus.

Akiyoshi Fukamizu and colleagues at the University of Tsukuba in Japan report in Friday's edition of the journal Science that they have managed to breed genetically altered mice that appear to experience a syndrome very similar to the problems seen in pregnant humans.

There are some differences between the human and mice models but the mice should provide more insight into the biochemistry of the disorder and possibly serve as a means of testing blood pressure medications.
"This is not the perfect model but it can give us some insights," Charles Rosenfeld, a neonatologist at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical School in Dallas, told Science.

The Japanese team did not set out to create a pre-eclampsia model. They were breeding genetically altered, or transgenic, mice to study high blood pressure in general and were using two human genes, one controlling a protein called angiotensinogen and the other making an enzyme called renin.

When female mice with the human renin gene were mated with males with the angiotensinogen alteration, the offspring had high blood pressure. When the scientists reversed the process -- mating females with human angiotensinogen and males with renin -- the mothers died late in pregnancy. Further study showed they had PIH-like symptoms, possibly because of the interaction of renin in the placenta with angiotensinogen in the mother.
